micro_skills.micro_skill: Single application of integration by parts: U=polynomial, dV=e^(ax), sin(ax), or cos(ax)
definitions: Integration by parts is inverse to the Product Rule: if U,V are differentiable, integral U dV = UV - integral V dU.
Rule of thumb: if the integrand is a polynomial times e^(ax), sin(ax), cos(ax), etc., let U=polynomial, dV=the rest.
formulas: integral U dV = UV - integral V dU

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a linear or simple polynomial factor times e^(ax), sin(ax), or cos(ax), needing exactly one application of integration by parts.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a degree-1 polynomial times an elementary function with a simple antiderivative — one application of IBP with U=x fully resolves it.
method_plan: Choose U=polynomial factor, dV=the remaining elementary factor times dx
Compute dU and V
Apply integral U dV = UV - integral V dU and evaluate the remaining integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct choice of U and dV with correct dU, V computed
M1: correct application of the IBP formula
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Choosing U and dV so the new integral is harder (e.g. U=e^(-x), dV=x dx), not easier
Sign error carrying through the -integral V dU term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a polynomial times a trig/exponential function with a LINEAR (not just x) argument, requiring extra care with the chain-rule factor in V.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The trig/exponential factor has a linear argument ax rather than plain x — V must include the resulting 1/a scaling factor.
method_plan: Choose U=polynomial, dV=trig/exponential(ax)dx
Compute V, remembering the 1/a scaling factor
Apply the IBP formula and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct V computed including the 1/a scaling factor
M1: correct application of the IBP formula
A1: correct final simplified antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the 1/a scaling factor when integrating the linear-argument trig/exponential function
Omitting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an integrand that superficially looks like an IBP candidate, decide whether IBP or a simple substitution is the efficient method.
question_archetypes.example: Compare integral x*e^x dx (IBP) with integral x*e^(x^2) dx (substitution, not IBP).
question_archetypes.answer: First needs IBP: (x-1)e^x+C. Second needs u=x^2 substitution: (1/2)e^(x^2)+C — IBP would not terminate usefully here.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: If the 'extra' factor is exactly the derivative (up to a constant) of the inner function of the other factor, substitution is faster than IBP; IBP is for genuine products of unrelated function types.
method_plan: Check whether one factor is proportional to the derivative of an expression inside the other factor
If so, use substitution; if not, apply IBP with the usual U/dV rules of thumb
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the applicable method
A1: correct execution and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Defaulting to IBP whenever a product is seen, without checking whether substitution is faster

micro_skills.micro_skill: Integration by parts with ln(x) or an inverse trig function as U (dV=dx or dV=polynomial dx)
definitions: Rule of thumb: if the integrand involves ln(x), an inverse trig function, or another factor that is easy to differentiate but hard/impossible to integrate directly, let that factor be U.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate ln(x) alone by using dV=dx (an 'invisible' choice), letting U=ln(x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is JUST ln(x) with no other visible factor — treat dV=dx (V=x) as the second factor.
method_plan: Let U=ln(x), dV=dx
Compute dU=dx/x, V=x
Apply the IBP formula, simplifying x*(1/x)=1, then integrate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct choice of U=ln(x), dV=dx
M1: correct dU, V computed
A1: correct simplification and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Not realizing dV=dx is a valid and necessary choice when only one function is visible
Error simplifying x*(1/x) in the resulting integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate an inverse trig function (e.g. arctan(x)) using U=arctan(x), dV=dx, then simplify the resulting rational-function integral.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is an inverse trig function alone — differentiate it (producing a rational function) rather than trying to integrate it directly.
method_plan: Let U=inverse trig function, dV=dx
Compute dU (a rational function) and V=x
Apply the IBP formula and evaluate the new integral (often via a quick substitution)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV, dU, V
M1: correct application of the IBP formula
A1: correct evaluation of the resulting rational-function integral
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Differentiation error finding dU for the inverse trig function
Not recognizing the resulting integral needs a further quick substitution before it can be evaluated

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a polynomial times ln(x), choosing U=ln(x) and dV=polynomial dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a polynomial (degree >=1) MULTIPLIED by ln(x) — U=ln(x), dV is the actual polynomial, since the polynomial is present and easy to integrate.
method_plan: Let U=ln(x), dV=polynomial dx
Compute dU=dx/x, V=antiderivative of the polynomial
Apply IBP, simplify (the x from V cancels with 1/x from dU), integrate, add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U=ln(x), dV=polynomial dx with correct V
M1: correct application of the IBP formula and simplification
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Choosing U=polynomial instead of U=ln(x), leaving ln(x) un-integrated in dV
Error simplifying the resulting polynomial integral after cancellation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate an inverse trig function whose derivative involves a square root (e.g. arcsin(x)), requiring a follow-up substitution to finish.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: U=sin^-1(x), dV=dx produces dU with a square root in the denominator; the resulting integral of x/sqrt(1-x^2) needs a quick u=1-x^2 substitution.
method_plan: Let U=sin^-1(x), dV=dx, compute dU and V=x
Apply IBP to get x*sin^-1(x) - integral x/sqrt(1-x^2) dx
Substitute u=1-x^2 to finish the remaining integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV, dU, V
M1: correct recognition and execution of the follow-up substitution
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the second integral requires its own substitution
Sign error in the substitution du=-2x dx

micro_skills.micro_skill: Polynomial (degree >=2) times exponential/trig function requiring repeated IBP, organized via the tabular (DI) method
definitions: The tabular (DI) method organizes repeated integration by parts: list successive derivatives of U (the polynomial, until it reaches 0) in one column and successive antiderivatives of dV in another, then sum diagonal products with alternating signs.
formulas: Tabular method: answer = sum of (sign)*(D-column entry)*(I-column entry, one row down)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a degree-2 polynomial times sin(ax) or cos(ax) using the tabular method (two applications of IBP).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Polynomial degree 2 times a trig/exponential function signals exactly 2 rounds of IBP — tabular method avoids re-deriving the formula twice.
method_plan: Build D-column: x^2, 2x, 2, 0; I-column: successive antiderivatives of sin(x)
Multiply diagonally with alternating signs (+,-,+) and sum
Add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct D-column (differentiates polynomial to 0)
M1: correct I-column (successive antiderivatives)
A1: correct alternating-sign diagonal sum with +C

common_errors.description: Stopping the table one row too early, before the polynomial column reaches 0
Alternating sign pattern applied incorrectly (e.g. all plus signs)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a degree-3 polynomial times e^(ax) using the tabular method (three applications of IBP).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Polynomial degree 3 means the D-column needs 4 rows (down to 0) — tabular method keeps repeated IBP organized and reduces arithmetic slips.
method_plan: Build D-column by differentiating the cubic down to 0
Build I-column by repeated antidifferentiation of e^(2x)
Sum diagonal products with alternating signs, add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct full D-column down to 0
M1: correct I-column with correct 1/2 scaling at each stage
A1: correct alternating-sign sum, simplified, with +C

common_errors.description: Losing track of the repeated 1/2 scaling factor from e^(2x) across three integrations
Misaligning which I-column row multiplies which D-column row

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize when the tabular method's D-column terminates (reaches exactly 0) and use that to know how many diagonal terms to sum.
question_archetypes.example: For integral x^2*e^(-3x) dx, identify how many rows the table needs.
question_archetypes.answer: 3 nonzero D-column rows (x^2, 2x, 2) plus the 0 row that stops the table; 3 product terms in the final sum.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The polynomial's degree tells you exactly how many derivatives until 0 — this determines the number of terms in the tabular sum, a quick self-check against dropped terms.
method_plan: Differentiate the polynomial repeatedly and note the degree at which it becomes 0
Confirm the table has that many nonzero product rows before stopping
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct count of nonzero rows tied to polynomial degree
A1: correctly stops the table at the 0 row without an extra or missing term

common_errors.description: Including an extra row after the D-column already reached 0

micro_skills.micro_skill: Repeated/cyclic IBP where the original integral I reappears after two applications; solve the resulting linear equation for I
definitions: A self-reproducing (cyclic) integral is one where two successive applications of IBP (keeping the SAME choice of which factor is U each time) return a multiple of the original integral I, giving a solvable linear equation for I.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate e^(ax) times sin(bx) or cos(bx) by applying IBP twice (consistently choosing the exponential as U both times) and solving for I.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is exponential times trig — neither factor 'runs out' under differentiation, so after 2 applications of IBP the original integral I reappears with a coefficient.
method_plan: Apply IBP once with U=e^(ax), keeping track of the new integral
Apply IBP again to the new integral, using U=e^(ax) again (consistent choice)
Recognize I reappears; solve the resulting linear equation for I algebraically, add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct first IBP application
M1: correct second IBP application with consistent U choice
A1: correct algebraic solution for I
A1: correct final simplified answer with +C

common_errors.description: Switching which factor is U between the first and second application, exactly undoing the first step instead of producing a solvable equation
Sign or coefficient error solving the linear equation for I

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive or apply the memorized reduction integral sec^3(x) dx using IBP with U=sec(x), dV=sec^2(x)dx, then a Pythagorean identity and solving for I.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: sec^3(x) splits naturally as sec(x)*sec^2(x); IBP produces a tan^2(x) term convertible via sec^2-1, after which I reappears.
method_plan: Let U=sec(x), dV=sec^2(x)dx, so dU=sec(x)tan(x)dx, V=tan(x)
Apply IBP, use tan^2(x)=sec^2(x)-1 to isolate I, and solve the linear equation
State the final memorized form with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV choice and IBP application
M1: correct use of the Pythagorean identity to reintroduce I
A1: correct algebraic solution for I with +C

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the Pythagorean identity is needed to reveal the reappearing I
Quoting the memorized result without deriving it when the question asks to derive it

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a partially-completed cyclic IBP calculation, identify the error where the choice of U was swapped between applications.
question_archetypes.example: A solution attempt for integral e^x*cos(x) dx swaps U from e^x to cos(x) on the second application and 'proves' 0=0. Identify the flaw.
question_archetypes.answer: Swapping U undoes the first IBP step algebraically, producing a true-but-useless identity (0=0) instead of an equation solvable for I; U must be chosen the same way (same factor type) on both applications.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A self-reproducing IBP setup that yields a trivial identity instead of an equation for I signals an inconsistent choice of U across applications.
method_plan: Redo the second IBP application keeping the same factor as U as in the first application
Confirm the resulting equation now contains I on both sides with different coefficients
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct diagnosis of the swapped-U error
A1: correct redo yielding a solvable equation for I

common_errors.description: Not understanding why consistent U choice is required for the cyclic method to work

micro_skills.micro_skill: Definite-integral integration by parts: evaluate the [UV] boundary term at both limits alongside the remaining integral
definitions: For a definite integral, integral_a^b U dV = [UV]_a^b - integral_a^b V dU, where [UV]_a^b = U(b)V(b) - U(a)V(a).
formulas: integral_a^b U dV = [UV]_a^b - integral_a^b V dU

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral by parts requiring exactly one application, evaluating the boundary term at both limits.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integral has specific numeric bounds — the boundary term UV must be evaluated at both limits, not carried along symbolically.
method_plan: Choose U, dV as in the indefinite case
Apply integral_a^b U dV = [UV]_a^b - integral_a^b V dU
Evaluate the boundary term at both limits and the remaining definite integral, then combine
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV, dU, V
M1: correct evaluation of the boundary term at both limits
A1: correct evaluation of the remaining definite integral
A1: correct final combined numeric value

common_errors.description: Forgetting to evaluate the [UV] boundary term at the limits (treating it as if this were an indefinite integral)
Sign error combining the boundary term with the remaining integral's value

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral requiring repeated IBP, tracking a boundary term at each stage.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Multiple rounds of IBP on a definite integral means multiple boundary terms accumulate — each must be evaluated at the same fixed limits.
method_plan: Perform repeated IBP (or use the tabular method) tracking boundary terms at each stage
Evaluate all boundary contributions at the given limits
Sum with the final remaining integral's evaluated value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct repeated IBP setup (or tabular method)
M1: correct evaluation of all boundary terms at the limits
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Evaluating only the final boundary term at the limits and forgetting earlier ones
Arithmetic slip evaluating e^0=1 or similar boundary values

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite IBP problem where the boundary term vanishes (e.g. due to a factor of 0 at both limits), simplifying to just the remaining integral.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_0^1 x*ln(x) dx (careful with the limit as x->0+).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A polynomial factor in U or V that is 0 at both endpoints (or a limit that vanishes, as x*ln(x)->0 as x->0+) makes the boundary term drop out entirely.
method_plan: Set up U, dV and compute the boundary term symbolically
Evaluate/take the limit of the boundary term at each endpoint, noting where it vanishes
Evaluate the remaining integral for the final answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV, dU, V
M1: correct justification that the boundary term vanishes (including any needed limit)
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Assuming the boundary term is automatically 0 without checking/justifying the limit at a singular endpoint

micro_skills.micro_skill: Derive and apply reduction formulas from integration by parts, expressing I_n in terms of I_(n-1) or I_(n-2)
definitions: A reduction formula expresses an integral I_n (depending on an integer parameter n) in terms of a similar integral I_(n-1) or I_(n-2) with a smaller parameter, obtained via one application of IBP; repeated use reduces I_n down to a known base case.

theorems.name: Wallis-type reduction for cos^n x
theorems.statement: For I_n = integral_0^(pi/2) cos^n(x) dx with n>=2: I_n = ((n-1)/n) I_(n-2), with I_0=pi/2, I_1=1.

formulas: I_n = integral x^n e^(-x) dx: I_n = -x^n*e^(-x) + n*I_(n-1)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive a reduction formula for I_n = integral x^n*e^(-ax) dx by applying IBP once with U=x^n.
question_archetypes.example: Derive a reduction formula for I_n = integral x^n*e^(-x) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integral has an integer parameter n in an exponent and the problem asks to relate I_n to I_(n-1) rather than compute directly.
method_plan: Let U=x^n, dV=e^(-ax)dx
Compute dU=n*x^(n-1)dx, V=(-1/a)e^(-ax)
Apply IBP and identify the resulting integral as I_(n-1) (up to a constant)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct U, dV, dU, V in terms of n
M1: correct IBP application
A1: correct final reduction formula relating I_n to I_(n-1)

common_errors.description: Losing track of the constant a or the factor of n from differentiating x^n

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a reduction formula, apply it repeatedly to evaluate I_n for a specific numeric n, down to a known base case.
question_archetypes.example: Given I_n = -x^n*e^(-x)+n*I_(n-1), find integral x^3*e^(-x) dx using I_0 = integral e^(-x)dx = -e^(-x)+C.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A reduction formula is given (or already derived) and a specific numeric n is requested — apply it recursively down to I_0 or I_1.
method_plan: Apply the reduction formula repeatedly, decrementing n each time
Substitute the known base case (I_0 or I_1)
Combine all terms into the final antiderivative with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct repeated application of the reduction formula
M1: correct base case substituted
A1: correct final simplified answer with +C

common_errors.description: Stopping the recursion one step early or late relative to the base case
Arithmetic slip combining terms across several recursive steps

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the Wallis-type reduction formula for integral_0^(pi/2) cos^n(x) dx to evaluate a specific even or odd power.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A definite integral of a power of sin or cos over 0 to pi/2 signals the Wallis reduction formula rather than repeated raw IBP.
method_plan: Apply I_n=((n-1)/n)I_(n-2) repeatedly down to I_0=pi/2 or I_1=1
Multiply the accumulated coefficients
State the final numeric value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct repeated application of the Wallis reduction
M1: correct base case (I_0 or I_1) used depending on parity of n
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Using the wrong base case (I_0 vs I_1) for the parity of n
Multiplying the chain of fractions incorrectly

micro_skills.micro_skill: Prepare a rational function for partial fractions: polynomial long division when deg P >= deg Q, plus basic linear/quadratic denominator antiderivatives
definitions: For integral P(x)/Q(x) dx: if deg P >= deg Q, perform polynomial long division first to write P/Q = (polynomial) + R(x)/Q(x) with deg R < deg Q, since partial fractions only applies to a proper rational function.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a rational function where deg P >= deg Q, requiring long division before partial fractions.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The numerator's degree is greater than or equal to the denominator's — partial fractions cannot be applied directly until long division produces a proper remainder.
method_plan: Perform polynomial long division: P/Q = polynomial + R/Q
Integrate the polynomial part directly
Apply partial fractions to the proper remainder R/Q and integrate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct long division performed
M1: correct partial fraction decomposition of the remainder
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Attempting partial fractions directly on an improper rational function without dividing first
Long division arithmetic error

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether long division is needed by comparing the degrees of numerator and denominator before decomposing.
question_archetypes.example: Is long division needed for integral (2x+3)/(x^2+x-6) dx?
question_archetypes.answer: No — deg numerator (1) < deg denominator (2), so partial fractions can be applied directly.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Comparing deg P and deg Q first avoids unnecessary work or a wrongly-skipped division step.
method_plan: Compare deg P to deg Q
If deg P < deg Q, proceed directly to partial fractions
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct degree comparison stated
A1: correct decision and correct decomposition

common_errors.description: Performing unnecessary long division, wasting time, when the rational function is already proper

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate directly using the basic quadratic-denominator formulas (x^2+a^2 or x^2-a^2 forms), splitting a numerator into an 'x' part and constant part first if needed.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The denominator is already an irreducible quadratic x^2+a^2 with no further factoring possible — split the numerator into a multiple of 2x (log form) plus a constant (arctan form) rather than setting up a full partial-fraction system.
method_plan: Write the numerator as a constant times the derivative of the denominator, plus a leftover constant
Integrate the log-form piece and the arctan-form piece separately
Combine and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct split of the numerator into derivative-matching and constant pieces
M1: correct application of both basic formulas
A1: correct final combined answer with +C

common_errors.description: Incorrect split of the numerator into the two required pieces
Using the x^2-a^2 formula (log form) when the denominator is x^2+a^2 (arctan form), or vice versa

micro_skills.micro_skill: Partial fraction decomposition with distinct (unrepeated) linear factors in the denominator
definitions: If Q(x) = K(x-a_1)(x-a_2)...(x-a_j) with all a_i distinct, then P(x)/Q(x) = A_1/(x-a_1) + ... + A_j/(x-a_j) for a proper rational function P/Q.

theorems.name: Cover-up method
theorems.statement: For a simple linear factor (x-a_j), multiply both sides by (x-a_j) and set x=a_j: A_j = P(a_j)/(product of (a_j-a_i) over i != j).
conditions: the factor (x-a_j) is linear and appears to the first power only

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function with two distinct linear factors using the cover-up method.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Denominator is already factored into two distinct linear factors — cover-up method quickly gives both constants.
method_plan: Set up A/(x-2) + B/(x-3)
Cover up each factor and evaluate the rest at its root to find A and B
Integrate each term as a log and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition form
M1: correct A and B via cover-up
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Evaluating at the wrong root when covering up a given factor
Missing absolute value bars in the log terms

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function with three or more distinct linear factors, using coefficient matching or repeated cover-up.
question_archetypes.answer: -2ln|x-1| - (1/3)... (coefficients found by cover-up at x=1, -1, 2) combined into A ln|x-1| + B ln|x+1| + C ln|x-2| + D
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three or more distinct linear factors means three or more unknowns — cover-up still works factor-by-factor since each is linear and unrepeated.
method_plan: Set up one unknown per linear factor
Find each constant via cover-up (or full coefficient matching as a check)
Integrate each log term and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition with correct number of unknowns
M1: correct constants found
A1: correct integration of each term with +C

common_errors.description: Arithmetic error evaluating P(a_j) or the product of root differences
Dropping one of the three required partial-fraction terms

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral of a rational function with distinct linear factors, being careful the interval avoids the poles.
question_archetypes.answer: -6ln(3) + 7ln(2) - (-6ln(2)+7ln(1)) simplified to a numeric value via [−6 ln|x−2|+7 ln|x−3|] from 4 to 5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Numeric bounds are given for a partial-fractions integral — check the interval doesn't contain a pole (x=2 or x=3) before evaluating via FTC.
method_plan: Decompose via cover-up as usual
Confirm the interval of integration contains no poles
Evaluate the antiderivative at both limits and subtract
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition and antiderivative
M1: confirmation the interval avoids poles (or correct treatment as improper if not)
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Evaluating a definite integral via FTC without checking whether a pole lies inside the interval

micro_skills.micro_skill: Partial fraction decomposition with a repeated linear factor (x-a)^m in the denominator
definitions: If (x-a)^m divides Q(x), the decomposition must include the full ladder A_1/(x-a) + A_2/(x-a)^2 + ... + A_m/(x-a)^m, not just a single term.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate integral P(x)/[(x-r)^k * Q(x)] dx where the denominator has one repeated linear factor.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A squared (or higher power) linear factor appears in the denominator — full ladder of terms up to that power is required.
method_plan: Set up A/x + B/(x-1) + C/(x-1)^2
Clear denominators, expand, match coefficients (or plug convenient x-values)
Integrate each term: linear terms give ln, repeated term gives -1/(x-1)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct partial-fraction setup with right number of unknowns
A1: correct coefficients
M1: correct integration of each term
A1: +C included, final answer simplified

common_errors.description: Only using one unknown for the repeated factor instead of the full ladder (missing the 1/(x-1)^2 term)
Forgetting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function whose denominator has both a repeated linear factor and a separate distinct linear factor.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Denominator factors into (x-a)^2 times a different linear factor — set up both the ladder for the repeated factor and a single term for the distinct one.
method_plan: Set up A/x + B/x^2 + C/(x-1)
Clear denominators and solve for A, B, C by matching coefficients or plugging in convenient values
Integrate each term and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition with correct terms for both the repeated and distinct factors
A1: correct coefficients solved
M1: correct integration of each term (including the -1/x-type term from 1/x^2)
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Sign error integrating 1/x^2 to -1/x
Omitting the plain A/x term when a repeated factor x^2 is present alongside the distinct factor

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a proposed (incomplete) partial fraction setup for a repeated linear factor, identify what term is missing.
question_archetypes.example: A student decomposes 1/(x(x-1)^2) as A/x + B/(x-1). What term is missing and why?
question_archetypes.answer: Missing C/(x-1)^2 — a repeated factor of multiplicity 2 requires terms for BOTH (x-1) and (x-1)^2, not just the first power.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Checking that the number of unknowns matches the total degree of the denominator (counting multiplicity) catches a missing-term error before solving.
method_plan: Count the total degree contributed by the repeated factor
Confirm one unknown exists per power up to that degree
Add the missing term and resolve
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the missing term
A1: correct corrected decomposition and resulting coefficients

common_errors.description: Believing one unknown per repeated factor suffices regardless of its power

micro_skills.micro_skill: Partial fraction decomposition with an irreducible (unrepeated) quadratic factor, using a linear numerator Bx+C
definitions: If (x^2+bx+c) is irreducible (no real roots) and appears once in Q(x), its partial-fraction term must have a LINEAR numerator: (Bx+C)/(x^2+bx+c), not just a constant.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function whose denominator is a linear factor times an irreducible quadratic.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral (2+3x+x^2)/(x(x^2+1)) dx... wait, use (x^2+2)/(x(x^2+1))-style example: integral (2+3x+x^2)/(x(x^2+1)) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Denominator factors into one linear factor times one irreducible quadratic — the quadratic's numerator must be Bx+C, not just C.
method_plan: Set up A/x + (Bx+C)/(x^2+1)
Clear denominators, expand, match coefficients
Split the quadratic term's integral into a log piece (from the x-part) and an arctan piece (from the constant part)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition with linear numerator over the quadratic
A1: correct coefficients A, B, C
M1: correct split and integration of the quadratic term
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Using only a constant numerator over the irreducible quadratic factor instead of a linear numerator Bx+C
Error splitting (Bx+C)/(x^2+1) into the log-form and arctan-form pieces

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function whose denominator is purely an irreducible quadratic (no linear factors at all).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The denominator does not factor over the reals at all — completing the square is required before splitting into log and arctan pieces (no partial-fraction system needed since there's only one term).
method_plan: Complete the square in the denominator
Split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the completed-square expression plus a constant
Integrate the log piece and the arctan piece separately, add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completing the square
M1: correct split of the numerator
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting to complete the square before attempting the arctan-form antiderivative
Error in the numerator split into derivative-matching and constant pieces

question_archetypes.prompt_template: After decomposing with an irreducible quadratic factor, simplify a final answer that combines multiple log terms into a single logarithm.
question_archetypes.example: Simplify 2ln|x| - (1/2)ln(x^2+1) + C into a single log expression.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A final answer with several log terms sharing the same base can often be combined using log laws — useful for matching an answer key's form.
method_plan: Rewrite each coefficient as an exponent inside the log (a*ln(u) = ln(u^a))
Combine using ln(u)-ln(v)=ln(u/v) or ln(u)+ln(v)=ln(uv)
State the single combined logarithmic expression plus the arctan term and +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rewriting of coefficients as exponents
A1: correct combination into a single log term
A1: correct final expression with +C

common_errors.description: Combining logs with different coefficient signs incorrectly
Dropping the separate arctan term when combining the log terms

micro_skills.micro_skill: Partial fraction decomposition with a repeated irreducible quadratic factor (x^2+bx+c)^n
definitions: If an irreducible quadratic factor (x^2+bx+c) is repeated n times, the decomposition needs a full ladder of linear-numerator terms: (B_1x+C_1)/(x^2+bx+c) + ... + (B_nx+C_n)/(x^2+bx+c)^n.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decompose and integrate a rational function with a repeated irreducible quadratic factor in the denominator.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A squared (or higher) irreducible quadratic factor appears — the full ladder with two linear-numerator terms (for power 1 and power 2) is required.
method_plan: Clear denominators and solve the resulting system for A through E
Integrate each term (the squared-denominator term typically integrates via a quick substitution) and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct full decomposition with both quadratic-ladder terms
A1: correct system solved for all constants
M1: correct integration of each term, including the (2x^2+1)^2 term
A1: correct final simplified answer with +C

common_errors.description: Using only one term for the repeated quadratic factor instead of the full two-term ladder
Error solving the larger coefficient-matching system with five unknowns

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given the decomposition setup for a repeated irreducible quadratic factor, solve the resulting system of equations for the unknown coefficients.
question_archetypes.example: Given x^2+2 = A(2x^2+1)^2 + (Bx+C)x(2x^2+1) + (Dx+E)x, solve for A, B, C, D, E.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Once the decomposition form is set up, matching coefficients of like powers of x (or plugging in strategic x-values plus matching a few coefficients) yields a linear system to solve.
method_plan: Expand the right-hand side fully
Match coefficients of each power of x on both sides
Solve the resulting linear system, using symmetry (odd powers) where possible to simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct expansion of the right-hand side
M1: correct system of equations from coefficient matching
A1: correct solved values for all unknowns

common_errors.description: Expansion error when multiplying out (2x^2+1)^2 or similar squared terms
Not exploiting symmetry (e.g. odd-degree terms vanishing) to simplify the system, making the solve unnecessarily long

micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize when a quadratic factor must be produced or simplified by completing the square before or after partial fractions
definitions: A quadratic that is not already in the form x^2+a^2 or x^2-a^2 (e.g. x^2-x+1) must be completed to the square, (x-h)^2+k, before its arctan/log antiderivative formulas can be applied.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Factor a sum-of-cubes-type denominator into a linear times an irreducible quadratic factor, then complete the square to integrate.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A cubic denominator that factors via sum/difference of cubes produces a linear factor times an irreducible quadratic that is not already a perfect x^2+a^2 form, requiring completing the square.
method_plan: Factor the denominator using the sum-of-cubes identity
Decompose into A/(x+1) + (Bx+C)/(x^2-x+1)
Complete the square in the quadratic factor, split the numerator, and integrate each piece
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct sum-of-cubes factorization
M1: correct partial fraction decomposition and coefficients
M1: correct completing the square and numerator split
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Sum-of-cubes factorization error (wrong sign in the quadratic factor)
Attempting to use the x^2+a^2 arctan formula directly without first completing the square

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a decomposed term (Bx+C)/(x^2+bx+c) with a non-perfect-square quadratic, complete the square and produce the combined log+arctan antiderivative.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The quadratic denominator has a linear term (bx term nonzero), signaling completing the square is needed to express the antiderivative in log+arctan form.
method_plan: Complete the square: x^2+bx+c = (x+b/2)^2 + k
Split the numerator into (derivative-matching multiple) + (constant)
Integrate: log term from the derivative-matching piece, arctan term (with the completed-square substitution) from the constant piece
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completing the square
M1: correct numerator split
A1: correct final answer combining log and arctan terms with +C

common_errors.description: Error completing the square (wrong value of k = c - b^2/4)
Using a instead of sqrt(k) inside the arctan after completing the square

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given several partial-fraction denominators, identify which ones require completing the square before integrating.
question_archetypes.example: Of x^2+4, x^2-x+1, and (x-3)^2, which needs completing the square first?
question_archetypes.answer: x^2-x+1 needs completing the square (it has a nonzero linear term and isn't already a perfect square); the other two are already in usable form.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A quadratic factor with a nonzero linear (bx) term that is irreducible signals the completing-the-square step is required before applying the standard formulas.
method_plan: Check each quadratic factor for a nonzero linear term
Complete the square only where needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of which factor(s) need completing the square
A1: correct completed-square form produced

common_errors.description: Completing the square unnecessarily on a denominator already in x^2+a^2 form, wasting time

micro_skills.micro_skill: Sine substitution x=a*sin(theta) for integrands containing sqrt(a^2-x^2)
definitions: For integrands containing sqrt(a^2-x^2), substitute x=a*sin(theta) (theta in [-pi/2,pi/2]); then 1-sin^2(theta)=cos^2(theta) gives sqrt(a^2-x^2)=a*cos(theta) and dx=a*cos(theta)d(theta).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(a^2-x^2) using the sine substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand contains sqrt(a^2-x^2) (or a power of it) with x^2 having a MINUS sign under the root — signals x=a*sin(theta).
method_plan: Substitute x=a*sin(theta), dx=a*cos(theta)d(theta), and simplify sqrt(a^2-x^2)=a*cos(theta)
Rewrite the integral entirely in theta and evaluate
Convert back to x using a right triangle (or sin^-1) for theta
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification of the square root
M1: correct evaluation of the resulting trig integral
A1: correct back-substitution to x with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert the final answer back from theta to x
Sign or coefficient error in dx=a*cos(theta)d(theta)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral with a fractional/negative power of (a^2-x^2), such as (a^2-x^2)^(-3/2), using the sine substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A power like (a^2-x^2)^(3/2) or its reciprocal in the denominator signals sine substitution, converting the power of cos(theta) into a simpler trig integral (often just sec^2(theta)).
method_plan: Substitute x=a*sin(theta), simplifying (a^2-x^2)^(power) to a power of a*cos(theta)
Simplify the resulting trig integral (cos(theta) terms cancel, often leaving sec^2(theta))
Integrate in theta and back-substitute to x via a right triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution with the power correctly simplified
M1: correct simplification/cancellation of cos(theta) factors
A1: correct final answer in terms of x with +C

common_errors.description: Incorrectly simplifying the power of cos(theta) after substitution

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral using the sine substitution, converting the x-limits into theta-limits.
question_archetypes.answer: Convert limits: x=0 => theta=0; x=3/2 => theta=pi/6; evaluate the resulting theta-integral over [0,pi/6] and simplify.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Numeric x-limits are given — with a trig substitution, converting the limits to theta at the outset (rather than substituting back to x) is usually more efficient for a definite integral.
method_plan: Convert the x-limits to theta-limits using x=a*sin(theta)
Substitute and simplify the integral entirely in theta
Evaluate directly at the theta-limits (no back-substitution to x needed)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct conversion of limits to theta
M1: correct substitution and simplification
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Reverting to x-limits and back-substituting theta to x unnecessarily instead of evaluating directly in theta
Error converting a specific x-value to the corresponding theta-value

micro_skills.micro_skill: Tangent substitution x=a*tan(theta) for integrands containing sqrt(a^2+x^2) or 1/(a^2+x^2)
definitions: For integrands containing sqrt(a^2+x^2) (or powers of a^2+x^2), substitute x=a*tan(theta) (theta in (-pi/2,pi/2)); then 1+tan^2(theta)=sec^2(theta) gives sqrt(a^2+x^2)=a*sec(theta) and dx=a*sec^2(theta)d(theta).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(a^2+x^2) using the tangent substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand contains sqrt(a^2+x^2) with a PLUS sign under the root — signals x=a*tan(theta), producing sec(theta) integrals.
method_plan: Substitute x=a*tan(theta), dx=a*sec^2(theta)d(theta), simplifying sqrt(a^2+x^2)=a*sec(theta)
Evaluate the resulting sec(theta) integral (memorized: ln|sec(theta)+tan(theta)|)
Convert back to x via a right triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification
M1: correct evaluation of the sec(theta) integral
A1: correct back-substitution to x with +C

common_errors.description: Not knowing/misremembering the integral of sec(theta)
Error converting sec(theta) and tan(theta) back to expressions in x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate integral dx/(a^2+x^2) or a related rational form using the tangent substitution (an alternative to memorizing the arctan formula directly).
question_archetypes.example: Derive integral dx/(x^2+4) using x=2tan(theta), confirming the arctan formula.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: 1/(a^2+x^2) is itself derivable via tangent substitution, reproducing the memorized arctan antiderivative — useful when the memorized formula is forgotten or when the numerator is more complex.
method_plan: Substitute x=a*tan(theta), simplifying a^2+x^2=a^2*sec^2(theta)
Simplify the resulting integral (the sec^2(theta) cancels, leaving a constant times d(theta))
Back-substitute theta=tan^-1(x/a)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification of a^2+x^2
M1: correct cancellation leaving a simple d(theta) integral
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the factor of 1/a arising from dx=a*sec^2(theta)d(theta) divided by a^2*sec^2(theta)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral with (a^2+x^2) raised to a higher power in the denominator, using tangent substitution and a resulting power of cos(theta).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A squared or higher power of (a^2+x^2) in the denominator, after tangent substitution, produces a power of cos(theta) requiring a half-angle or reduction technique to finish.
method_plan: Substitute x=a*tan(theta), simplifying (a^2+x^2)^n to a power of sec(theta)
Simplify to a power of cos(theta) and integrate using a half-angle identity or reduction formula
Back-substitute to x via a right triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and power simplification
M1: correct integration of the resulting power of cos(theta)
A1: correct back-substitution and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the need for a half-angle identity when integrating an even power of cos(theta)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Secant substitution x=a*sec(theta) for integrands containing sqrt(x^2-a^2), with attention to the branch/sign of the result
definitions: For integrands containing sqrt(x^2-a^2) (x>=a or x<=-a), substitute x=a*sec(theta); then sec^2(theta)-1=tan^2(theta) gives sqrt(x^2-a^2)=a|tan(theta)|, whose sign depends on which branch (x>=a or x<=-a) is in play.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(x^2-a^2), for x>a, using the secant substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand contains sqrt(x^2-a^2) with x^2 having a PLUS sign but a MINUS a^2 under the root — signals x=a*sec(theta).
method_plan: Substitute x=a*sec(theta), dx=a*sec(theta)tan(theta)d(theta), simplify sqrt(x^2-a^2)=a*tan(theta) (for x>a)
Evaluate the resulting sec(theta) integral
Back-substitute to x via a right triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification for the given branch
M1: correct evaluation of the resulting integral
A1: correct back-substitution with +C

common_errors.description: Sign error in sqrt(sec^2(theta)-1)=|tan(theta)| when not confirming the branch
Not simplifying dx and the square root together correctly before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(x^2-a^2) where x<=-a, requiring the opposite sign branch of the secant substitution result.
question_archetypes.answer: Result mirrors the x>=2 case but with an extra sign flip from tan(theta)=-sqrt(x^2-4)/2 on this branch; final antiderivative form is the same up to sign, expressed via |x|.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The domain restriction is x<=-a rather than x>=a — the sign relating sqrt(x^2-a^2) to a*tan(theta) flips, and this must be tracked explicitly or handled via absolute values.
method_plan: Identify which branch (x>=a or x<=-a) applies from the problem's domain
Substitute x=a*sec(theta) with theta restricted to the correct interval for that branch
Carry the correct sign through simplification and back-substitution
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the branch and corresponding theta interval
M1: correct sign carried through the simplification
A1: correct final answer valid for the given domain

common_errors.description: Using the x>=a sign convention on an x<=-a problem without adjusting

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral where sqrt(x^2-a^2) appears in combination with other algebraic factors (e.g. x^2 in the denominator), using secant substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: sqrt(x^2-a^2) combined with additional powers of x elsewhere in the integrand still signals secant substitution; simplify all factors (including the extra x powers) in terms of theta together.
method_plan: Substitute x=a*sec(theta) throughout the entire integrand, not just the square root
Simplify the resulting trig integral (often reduces to a single cos(theta) or similar term)
Back-substitute to x via a right triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution applied to every factor in the integrand
M1: correct simplification of the resulting trig expression
A1: correct back-substitution and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Substituting into the square root correctly but forgetting to substitute into other x-factors in the integrand

micro_skills.micro_skill: Hyperbolic substitutions (x=a*cosh(u) or x=a*sinh(u)) as an alternative to secant/sine substitutions, avoiding absolute-value branch issues
definitions: For sqrt(x^2-a^2) (x>=a), x=a*cosh(u) gives sqrt(x^2-a^2)=a*sinh(u) (no sign ambiguity since cosh(u)>=1, sinh(u)>=0 for u>=0). For sqrt(a^2+x^2), x=a*sinh(u) gives sqrt(a^2+x^2)=a*cosh(u).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(x^2-a^2) (x>=a) using the hyperbolic cosh substitution instead of secant.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral dx/sqrt(x^2-a^2) for x>=a>0 via x=a*cosh(u).
question_archetypes.answer: u + C = cosh^-1(x/a) + C, equivalent to ln|x+sqrt(x^2-a^2)| + C_1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: sqrt(x^2-a^2) can be handled with x=a*cosh(u), avoiding the absolute-value/branch subtlety of secant since cosh(u)>=1 and sinh(u)>=0 automatically for the principal branch.
method_plan: Substitute x=a*cosh(u), dx=a*sinh(u)du, simplify sqrt(x^2-a^2)=a*sinh(u)
Evaluate the (usually simpler) resulting integral in u
Back-substitute u=cosh^-1(x/a), optionally converting to the equivalent log form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification
M1: correct evaluation of the resulting integral in u
A1: correct back-substitution with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the domain restriction x>=a needed for the cosh substitution to be valid
Leaving the answer in terms of u instead of converting back to x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(a^2+x^2) using the hyperbolic sinh substitution instead of tangent.
question_archetypes.answer: u + C = sinh^-1(x/a) + C, equivalent to ln(x+sqrt(a^2+x^2)) + C_1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: sqrt(a^2+x^2) can be handled with x=a*sinh(u) since sinh is defined and invertible for all real x, avoiding branch cases entirely (unlike sec/tan for the other root types).
method_plan: Substitute x=a*sinh(u), dx=a*cosh(u)du, simplify sqrt(a^2+x^2)=a*cosh(u)
Evaluate the resulting integral in u
Back-substitute u=sinh^-1(x/a) or the equivalent log form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and simplification
M1: correct evaluation of the resulting integral
A1: correct back-substitution with +C

common_errors.description: Confusing the identity cosh^2(u)-sinh^2(u)=1 direction (using it as sinh^2-cosh^2=1)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show that the hyperbolic-substitution result and the trig-substitution result for the same integral are equivalent (differ only by a constant or algebraic rearrangement).
question_archetypes.example: Show integral dx/sqrt(x^2-a^2) gives ln|x+sqrt(x^2-a^2)|+C via secant substitution and cosh^-1(x/a)+C via hyperbolic substitution are equivalent.
question_archetypes.answer: Using cosh^-1(t)=ln(t+sqrt(t^2-1)), cosh^-1(x/a)=ln(x/a+sqrt(x^2/a^2-1))=ln(x+sqrt(x^2-a^2))-ln(a), which differs from the secant-substitution result only by the constant -ln(a), absorbed into C.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two different valid substitution methods on the same integral should give answers differing at most by an additive constant — a useful check when results look different on the surface.
method_plan: Express cosh^-1 or sinh^-1 in terms of a natural log using its definition
Algebraically compare to the log form obtained from the trig substitution
Show the difference is an additive constant, hence both are valid antiderivatives
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct log-form definition of the inverse hyperbolic function used
A1: correct algebraic demonstration the two results agree up to a constant

common_errors.description: Assuming two differently-shaped correct antiderivatives must indicate an error, rather than checking they differ by a constant

micro_skills.micro_skill: Rationalizing substitutions for integrands with roots: single fractional power, nth root, or several different fractional powers (lcm substitution)
definitions: For sqrt(ax+b), substitute ax+b=u^2 (or more generally ax+b=u^n for an nth root) to rationalize; for several different fractional powers x^(1/p), x^(1/q), ..., substitute x=u^m where m=lcm(p,q,...) to rationalize all of them simultaneously.
formulas: ax+b=u^n rationalizes an nth root; x=u^(lcm(p,q,...)) rationalizes several fractional powers x^(1/p), x^(1/q), ...

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing sqrt(ax+b) using the substitution ax+b=u^2.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral x*sqrt(x+1) dx via u^2=x+1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A single square-root expression sqrt(ax+b) (not a difference or sum of squares under the root) signals a direct rationalizing substitution rather than a trig substitution.
method_plan: Substitute u^2=ax+b (or u=sqrt(ax+b)), solving for x and dx in terms of u
Rewrite the entire integrand as a polynomial (or simple rational function) in u
Integrate in u and back-substitute u=sqrt(ax+b)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution with x and dx expressed in terms of u
M1: correct rewriting of the full integrand in u
A1: correct back-substitution and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting to also substitute for the OTHER x factor (e.g. the plain x in x*sqrt(x+1)), not just the root

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing an nth root, sqrt[n]{ax+b}, using the substitution ax+b=u^n.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A cube root or other nth root (not a square root) appears in the integrand — substitute so the root becomes u itself, clearing it entirely.
method_plan: Substitute ax+b=u^n, solving for x and dx in terms of u
Rewrite the integrand as a rational function of u (often requiring polynomial long division)
Integrate (commonly via partial fractions or log/polynomial terms) and back-substitute
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution clearing the nth root
M1: correct rewriting as a rational function of u, including any needed long division
A1: correct final answer back in terms of x with +C

common_errors.description: Not performing long division on the resulting improper rational function of u before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral containing several different fractional powers of x by substituting x=u^m with m the least common multiple of the denominators.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand contains two or more DIFFERENT fractional powers of x (e.g. x^(1/2) and x^(1/3)) — a single substitution x=u^(lcm of denominators) rationalizes all of them at once.
method_plan: Find m=lcm of all the denominators of the fractional exponents
Substitute x=u^m, dx=m*u^(m-1)du, rewriting every fractional power as an integer power of u
Integrate the resulting rational function of u and back-substitute u=x^(1/m)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct lcm found and substitution set up
M1: correct rewriting of every fractional power as an integer power of u
A1: correct integration and back-substitution with +C

common_errors.description: Using an m that is a common multiple but not the LEAST common multiple, leading to unnecessarily high powers
Error rewriting one of the fractional powers in terms of u after substitution

micro_skills.micro_skill: Weierstrass substitution x=tan(theta/2) converting any rational function of sin(theta), cos(theta) into a rational function of x
definitions: The Weierstrass (tan half-angle) substitution sets x=tan(theta/2); then cos(theta)=(1-x^2)/(1+x^2), sin(theta)=2x/(1+x^2), and d(theta)=2dx/(1+x^2). This converts ANY rational function of sin(theta) and cos(theta) into a rational function of x, integrable by Section 6.2's partial-fraction methods.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral of a rational function of sin(theta) and cos(theta) using the Weierstrass substitution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a rational function combining sin(theta) and/or cos(theta) in a way that no simple substitution or identity resolves directly — the universal Weierstrass substitution always applies.
method_plan: Substitute x=tan(theta/2), replacing cos(theta), sin(theta), and d(theta) with their x-formulas
Simplify to a rational function of x and integrate using partial fractions or basic quadratic-denominator formulas
Back-substitute x=tan(theta/2)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution formulas for cos(theta), sin(theta), d(theta)
M1: correct simplification to a rational function of x
A1: correct integration of the rational function
A1: correct back-substitution with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the d(theta)=2dx/(1+x^2) factor when converting the differential
Error substituting cos(theta) or sin(theta) into the denominator and simplifying the resulting fraction

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral of a rational trig function using the Weierstrass substitution, converting theta-limits to x-limits.
question_archetypes.answer: Convert limits theta=0 => x=0, theta=pi/2 => x=1; integrate 2/(1+x)^2 dx from 0 to 1, giving 1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Numeric theta-limits with a rational sin/cos integrand — convert limits to x=tan(theta/2) values at the outset rather than substituting back at the end.
method_plan: Convert the theta-limits to x-limits via x=tan(theta/2)
Substitute and simplify the integral entirely in x
Evaluate directly at the x-limits
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limit conversion
M1: correct substitution and simplification
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Error converting a specific theta-value (e.g. pi/2) to the corresponding x=tan(theta/2) value

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Decide whether a rational-trig integral needs the general Weierstrass substitution or can be solved faster with a simpler identity/substitution.
question_archetypes.example: Compare integral d(theta)/(2+cos(theta)) (needs Weierstrass) with integral sin(theta)cos(theta)d(theta) (simpler direct substitution u=sin(theta)).
question_archetypes.answer: The first genuinely needs Weierstrass since no simple identity simplifies 1/(2+cos(theta)); the second is faster with u=sin(theta) directly, without invoking the general method.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: If a quick identity or ordinary substitution (like u=sin(theta) when cos(theta)d(theta) is present) resolves the integral, prefer it — reserve Weierstrass for integrands where sin/cos are mixed in the denominator or combined in a way no simple identity clears.
method_plan: Check whether a direct substitution or identity already simplifies the integral
Only invoke the Weierstrass substitution when no simpler method applies
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct assessment of whether a simpler method suffices
A1: correct execution of whichever method is chosen

common_errors.description: Defaulting to the (algebraically heavier) Weierstrass substitution when a much simpler identity-based substitution would suffice

micro_skills.micro_skill: Guess-and-match antiderivative of P(x)*e^(ax) as Q(x)*e^(ax) with Q a same-degree polynomial
definitions: For integral P(x)e^(ax)dx with P a polynomial of degree n, guess the antiderivative is Q(x)e^(ax) with Q also a polynomial of degree n (the family x^k*e^(ax) is closed under differentiation); differentiate the guess and match coefficients against P(x).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use undetermined coefficients to integrate a quadratic (or higher) polynomial times e^x, guessing a same-degree polynomial times e^x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a polynomial times e^(ax) — instead of repeated IBP, guess the antiderivative has the same polynomial degree times e^(ax) and solve for coefficients directly.
method_plan: Guess I=(a_0+a_1x+...+a_nx^n)e^(ax)
Differentiate the guess and set equal to the original integrand
Match coefficients of each power of x to solve for all a_k
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct guess with matching polynomial degree
M1: correct differentiation of the guess
A1: correct coefficients solved via matching
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Guessing a polynomial degree too low, not matching the highest power present in the integrand
Error differentiating the guessed product and collecting like terms

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a claimed antiderivative found via undetermined coefficients, verify it by differentiating and comparing to the original integrand.
question_archetypes.example: Verify that (x^2-x+2)e^x is an antiderivative of (x^2+x+1)e^x.
question_archetypes.answer: Differentiating (x^2-x+2)e^x via product rule gives (2x-1)e^x+(x^2-x+2)e^x=(x^2+x+1)e^x, confirming the result.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A quick differentiation check confirms an undetermined-coefficients answer without redoing the whole coefficient-matching process — good exam-time sanity check.
method_plan: Differentiate the claimed antiderivative using the product rule
Simplify and compare to the original integrand
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct differentiation via the product rule
A1: correct confirmation matching the original integrand

common_errors.description: Not verifying the final answer by differentiation when time permits, missing an easy error check

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a high-degree polynomial times e^(ax), compare the efficiency of undetermined coefficients versus repeated IBP/tabular method.
question_archetypes.example: For integral (x^4+3x^2-1)e^(-2x) dx, discuss why undetermined coefficients may be preferable to 4 rounds of IBP.
question_archetypes.answer: Undetermined coefficients requires solving one linear system (5 unknowns) in a single pass, while repeated IBP/tabular requires 4 careful sequential applications — for high degree, the system approach is often less error-prone despite more algebra upfront.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: For high polynomial degree, the number of required IBP applications grows linearly, while undetermined coefficients converts this into a single (larger) linear system — a strategic trade-off worth recognizing.
method_plan: Set up the undetermined-coefficients guess with unknowns matching the polynomial degree
Differentiate and match coefficients to form the linear system
Solve the system (often triangular, back-substitutable from the highest power down)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct guess and differentiation
M1: correct system of equations set up in triangular form
A1: correct coefficients solved by back-substitution

common_errors.description: Choosing repeated IBP for a high-degree polynomial when undetermined coefficients would be faster and less error-prone

micro_skills.micro_skill: Guess-and-match antiderivative of x^m*cos(ax) or x^m*sin(ax) as Q(x)cos(ax)+R(x)sin(ax)
definitions: For integral x^m*cos(ax)dx or integral x^m*sin(ax)dx, guess the antiderivative is Q(x)cos(ax)+R(x)sin(ax) with Q,R polynomials of degree m (the family is closed under differentiation as a pair); differentiate and match coefficients.
formulas: integral x^m cos(ax)dx or integral x^m sin(ax)dx = Q(x)cos(ax)+R(x)sin(ax)+C, deg(Q)=deg(R)=m

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use undetermined coefficients to integrate a linear or quadratic polynomial times cos(ax) or sin(ax).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral x*sin(2x) dx via undetermined coefficients: guess I=(a+bx)cos(2x)+(c+dx)sin(2x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a polynomial times a single trig function — since differentiating cos(ax) or sin(ax) swaps between them, the guess must include BOTH cos and sin terms, each with a degree-m polynomial coefficient.
method_plan: Guess I=Q(x)cos(ax)+R(x)sin(ax) with Q,R of the same degree as the polynomial in the integrand
Differentiate the guess and match coefficients of x^k*cos(ax) and x^k*sin(ax) separately
Solve for all coefficients and state the final answer with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct guess including both cos and sin polynomial terms
M1: correct differentiation of the guess
A1: correct coefficients solved
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Guessing only a cos(ax) term (or only sin) without including the other, since differentiating one produces the other
Sign error differentiating cos(ax) to -a*sin(ax)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use undetermined coefficients to integrate a higher-degree polynomial times cos(ax) or sin(ax), solving a larger coefficient system.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral x^2*cos(x) dx via undetermined coefficients.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Higher polynomial degree means more unknowns in Q(x) and R(x) — the coefficient-matching system grows but remains systematically solvable degree by degree, from the top down.
method_plan: Guess I=Q(x)cos(ax)+R(x)sin(ax) with Q,R of the matching higher degree
Differentiate and match coefficients level by level, starting from the highest power
Solve the resulting (typically triangular) system for all unknowns
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct guess of matching degree
M1: correct systematic coefficient matching from highest degree down
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Losing track of which equation corresponds to which power of x when the system grows large

micro_skills.micro_skill: Guess-and-match antiderivative of x^m*(ln x)^n as x^(m+1) times a degree-n polynomial in ln(x)
definitions: For integral x^m(ln x)^n dx, guess the antiderivative is x^(m+1)*sum_{k=0}^{n} c_k(ln x)^k (a polynomial in ln x of the same degree n, times x^(m+1)); differentiate and match coefficients of each x^m(ln x)^k term.
formulas: integral x^m(ln x)^n dx = x^(m+1)*sum_{k=0}^{n} c_k(ln x)^k + C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use undetermined coefficients to integrate x^m(ln x)^n for a small n (e.g. n=2), as an alternative to repeated IBP.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A polynomial times a POWER of ln(x) (not just ln(x) alone) signals guessing a degree-n polynomial in ln(x), times x^(m+1), rather than doing n rounds of IBP by hand.
method_plan: Guess I=x^(m+1)(P*(ln x)^n + Q*(ln x)^(n-1) + ... + constant term)
Differentiate the guess (product and chain rule) and match coefficients of each x^m(ln x)^k term
Solve for all coefficients from the top power of ln(x) down
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct guess with the right degree-n polynomial in ln(x)
M1: correct differentiation of the guess
A1: correct coefficients solved level by level
A1: correct final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Guessing a polynomial in ln(x) of the wrong degree (not matching n)
Product/chain rule error differentiating x^(m+1)(ln x)^k

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given the undetermined-coefficients setup for x^m(ln x)^n, solve the resulting triangular system for the coefficients from top degree down.
question_archetypes.example: Given I=Px^4(ln x)^2+Qx^4 ln x+Rx^4 for integral x^3(ln x)^2 dx, solve for P, Q, R.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The system from matching (ln x)^k coefficients is naturally triangular — the highest power of ln(x) determines its coefficient first, then each lower one in turn.
method_plan: Match the coefficient of the highest power of ln(x) first to solve the top unknown
Substitute down to solve each successively lower coefficient
Confirm the constant term last
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct top-level coefficient solved first
A1: correct remaining coefficients solved by back-substitution

common_errors.description: Attempting to solve all coefficients simultaneously instead of top-down, causing avoidable algebra errors

micro_skills.subtopic: Integral Tables, Technology, and Non-Elementary Integrals
micro_skills.micro_skill: Use integral tables/CAS after massaging an integral into a listed form, and recognize non-elementary integrals defined via special functions
definitions: Integral tables (often built from reduction formulas) and computer algebra systems can evaluate integrals symbolically, but typically require first massaging the integral (via substitution) into a form matching a table entry.
Some integrals — such as integral e^(-x^2)dx — provably have no elementary closed form; they define new special functions, e.g. the error function erf(x) = (2/sqrt(pi)) * integral_0^x e^(-t^2) dt.
formulas: integral e^(-x^2)dx = (sqrt(pi)/2)*erf(x) + C, where erf(x)=(2/sqrt(pi))integral_0^x e^(-t^2)dt

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an integral table entry and a target integral not quite in that form, apply a substitution first to match the table entry.
question_archetypes.example: Given a table entry for integral dx/sqrt(u^2+a^2) = ln(u+sqrt(u^2+a^2))+C, evaluate integral dx/sqrt(4x^2+9) by substituting u=2x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integral resembles a table entry but with a scaled or shifted variable — a quick substitution (often linear) puts it exactly into the tabulated form.
method_plan: Identify which table entry the integral resembles
Apply a substitution (e.g. u=linear expression) to match the table form exactly, tracking the resulting constant factor
Apply the table formula and back-substitute
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the relevant table entry
M1: correct substitution to match the table form
A1: correct back-substitution and final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the extra constant factor introduced by the substitution needed to match the table form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine that a given integral has no elementary closed-form antiderivative and must be expressed via a special function or left as a definite integral.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why integral e^(-x^2) dx cannot be expressed in elementary closed form.
question_archetypes.answer: It is a proven (non-obvious) result that e^(-x^2) has no elementary antiderivative; the integral defines the (non-elementary) error function erf(x) up to a constant multiple.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Certain classic integrands (e^(-x^2), sin(x)/x, 1/ln(x), etc.) are known to lack elementary antiderivatives — recognize these rather than attempting fruitless algebraic manipulation.
method_plan: Recognize the integrand as one of the classic non-elementary cases
State the result in terms of the corresponding special function (e.g. erf) rather than searching for an elementary form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct recognition that no elementary antiderivative exists
A1: correct expression using the appropriate special function

common_errors.description: Spending excessive time trying substitutions/IBP on a known non-elementary integral instead of recognizing it and using the special-function definition

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Express a definite integral of e^(-x^2) (or a related Gaussian-type integrand) in terms of the error function.
question_archetypes.example: Express integral_0^2 e^(-x^2) dx in terms of erf.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A definite integral of e^(-x^2) or e^(-ax^2) over finite limits, when an exact elementary value is requested but impossible, should be expressed via erf rather than left unevaluated or approximated without justification.
method_plan: Recognize the Gaussian-type integrand as non-elementary
Relate the definite integral to the error function definition, adjusting for any scaling constant
State the final answer in terms of erf evaluated at the limits
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct recognition of the non-elementary integrand
A1: correct expression in terms of erf with correct scaling

common_errors.description: Attempting to find an elementary closed form instead of expressing the answer via erf

micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate Type I improper integrals (infinite interval) as a limit of proper integrals
definitions: integral_a^infinity f(x)dx = lim_{R->infinity} integral_a^R f(x)dx, and similarly integral_{-infinity}^b f(x)dx = lim_{R->-infinity} integral_R^b f(x)dx. integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} f dx splits into integral_{-infinity}^0 f dx + integral_0^infinity f dx; BOTH pieces must converge for the whole to converge.

If the limit is finite, the integral converges; if the limit fails to exist as a finite number, the integral diverges (to +/-infinity if the limit is infinite; otherwise it just diverges, e.g. if it oscillates).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a Type I improper integral over a single infinite interval by taking the limit of a proper integral.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The upper (or lower) limit of integration is infinity — replace it with a variable R, evaluate the proper integral, then take the limit as R->infinity.
method_plan: Replace infinity with a finite variable R (or -R)
Evaluate the resulting proper definite integral via the antiderivative
Take the limit as R->infinity (or -infinity) and state convergence or divergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct setup as a limit of a proper integral
M1: correct antiderivative and evaluation at the limits
A1: correct limit taken and convergence/divergence stated with the correct value

common_errors.description: Applying the Fundamental Theorem directly by 'plugging in infinity' without taking a genuine limit
Not explicitly stating whether the integral converges or diverges

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} f(x)dx by splitting at a finite point and requiring BOTH resulting pieces to converge independently.
question_archetypes.answer: pi (each half contributes pi/2, both converge)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both limits of integration are infinite — split at any convenient finite point (e.g. 0) into two separate Type I integrals, each with its own independent limit.
method_plan: Split the integral at a finite point into two pieces, each with one infinite limit
Evaluate each piece as its own limit
Confirm both pieces converge before adding; if either diverges, the whole diverges
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct split into two Type I integrals
M1: correct evaluation of each piece's limit
A1: correct conclusion (convergent sum, or divergence if either piece fails) with correct value

common_errors.description: Evaluating integral_{-R}^{R} f dx and taking a single limit as R->infinity (a 'principal value'), incorrectly treating it as proof of convergence even when the two-sided split would diverge
Only checking one of the two pieces for convergence

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a Type I improper integral that diverges (to infinity, or by oscillation) and correctly state the type of divergence.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_1^infinity dx/x, and separately integral_0^infinity cos(x)dx.
question_archetypes.answer: integral_1^infinity dx/x diverges to infinity (lim of ln R); integral_0^infinity cos(x)dx diverges by oscillation (lim of sin R does not exist).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Not all divergent improper integrals diverge 'to infinity' — some limits simply fail to exist (oscillate), which must be stated as 'diverges' rather than 'diverges to infinity'.
method_plan: Set up the limit of the proper integral as usual
Determine whether the limit is infinite, or simply does not exist
State the precise form of divergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limit setup and evaluation attempt
A1: correct precise statement of divergence type (to infinity vs. oscillating/no limit)

common_errors.description: Stating 'diverges to infinity' for an oscillating integral where the limit simply does not exist

micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate Type II improper integrals (unbounded integrand) as a limit, splitting at any interior singularity
definitions: If f is unbounded near a (continuous on (a,b]): integral_a^b f(x)dx = lim_{c->a+} integral_c^b f(x)dx, and similarly if unbounded near b. If f is unbounded at an interior point (or at both ends), split into separate improper integrals at each singularity.
formulas: integral_a^b f(x)dx = lim_{c->a+} integral_c^b f(x)dx  [f unbounded near a]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a Type II improper integral where the integrand is unbounded at one endpoint of the interval.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand blows up (denominator -> 0, or similar) at one of the stated limits of integration — replace that limit with a variable approaching it and take a one-sided limit.
method_plan: Identify which endpoint the integrand is unbounded at
Replace that endpoint with a variable c and take the appropriate one-sided limit
Evaluate and state convergence/divergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the singular endpoint
M1: correct limit setup and evaluation
A1: correct convergence/divergence conclusion with correct value

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the integrand is unbounded at an endpoint, applying the FTC as if the integral were proper
Taking the limit from the wrong side (e.g. c->a- instead of c->a+)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral where the integrand is unbounded at an INTERIOR point, requiring a split there before taking any limits.
question_archetypes.example: Determine whether integral_{-1}^1 dx/x^2 converges (interior singularity at x=0).
question_archetypes.answer: Diverges — splitting at x=0 gives integral_{-1}^0 dx/x^2 + integral_0^1 dx/x^2, and each piece individually diverges to infinity ($p=2\ge1$), so the whole diverges.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is unbounded at a point STRICTLY INSIDE the interval of integration, not just at an endpoint — must split there into two separate improper integrals before evaluating either.
method_plan: Locate the interior point where the integrand is unbounded
Split the integral into two pieces at that point
Evaluate each piece as its own one-sided limit; the whole converges only if both pieces converge
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the interior singularity
M1: correct split into two separate improper integrals
A1: correct evaluation/convergence determination of each piece
A1: correct final conclusion for the combined integral

common_errors.description: Applying the FTC directly across the interior singularity without splitting (this can produce a plausible-looking but meaningless finite 'answer')
Splitting at the singularity but only checking one of the two resulting pieces for convergence

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral that is improper in BOTH senses (an infinite limit of integration AND an unbounded integrand within the interval), requiring splitting at every problem point.
question_archetypes.answer: Converges — split at x=1: near 0 compare to x^{-1/2} (p=1/2<1, converges); near infinity compare to x^{-3/2} (p=3/2>1, converges); both pieces converge so the whole converges.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An integral can be improper for more than one reason simultaneously (an infinite endpoint plus a singularity elsewhere) — identify and split at every distinct problem point before analyzing each piece.
method_plan: Identify every source of impropriety (infinite limit(s), unbounded integrand point(s))
Split the integral at a convenient interior point so each piece has exactly one source of impropriety
Analyze each piece separately (often via comparison) and combine the conclusions
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of all sources of impropriety
M1: correct split isolating each one
A1: correct analysis of each piece
A1: correct overall conclusion

common_errors.description: Only identifying one of the two sources of impropriety and ignoring the other

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply the p-integral test to determine convergence of integral x^(-p) over an infinite interval or near a finite singularity
definitions: For 0<a<infinity: integral_a^infinity x^(-p)dx converges (to a^(1-p)/(p-1)) iff p>1, and diverges to infinity if p<=1. integral_0^a x^(-p)dx converges (to a^(1-p)/(1-p)) iff p<1, and diverges to infinity if p>=1.

theorems.name: p-Integral Test
theorems.statement: integral_a^infinity x^(-p)dx converges iff p>1; integral_0^a x^(-p)dx converges iff p<1.
conditions: the exponent -p applies to x alone (or a shifted/scaled version of x)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine convergence of a p-integral over an infinite interval and evaluate it if convergent.
question_archetypes.example: Determine whether integral_2^infinity dx/x^3 converges, and if so, evaluate it.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a pure power x^(-p) (or reduces to one) over an infinite interval — apply the p>1 threshold directly rather than computing the limit from scratch.
method_plan: Identify p from the exponent of x
