Apply the threshold p>1 for convergence on an infinite interval
If convergent, evaluate using the closed-form value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of p
M1: correct application of the p>1 threshold
A1: correct evaluated value (or correctly stated divergence)

common_errors.description: Using the wrong threshold direction (thinking p<1 converges on an infinite interval, which is the finite-interval rule)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine convergence of a p-integral with a singularity at a finite endpoint (e.g. x=0) and evaluate it if convergent.
question_archetypes.example: Determine whether integral_0^1 dx/x^(2/3) converges, and if so, evaluate it.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a pure power x^(-p) with a singularity at a finite endpoint — apply the p<1 threshold (opposite direction from the infinite-interval case).
method_plan: Identify p from the exponent of x
Apply the threshold p<1 for convergence near a finite singularity
If convergent, evaluate using the closed-form value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of p
M1: correct application of the p<1 threshold
A1: correct evaluated value (or correctly stated divergence)

common_errors.description: Confusing this with the infinite-interval threshold (using p>1 instead of p<1)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply the Comparison Test (and asymptotic/big-O comparison) to determine convergence or divergence without evaluating the integral exactly
definitions: If 0<=f(x)<=g(x) on the (possibly improper) interval (a,b): integral g converges implies integral f converges (and is <= integral g); integral f diverges to infinity implies integral g diverges to infinity.
Big-O comparison: if f(x)=O(x^(-p)) as x->infinity with p>1, then integral_1^infinity f dx converges (compare to a p-integral); similarly near a finite singularity with p<1.

theorems.name: Comparison Test for Improper Integrals
theorems.statement: If 0<=f(x)<=g(x) on the interval and integral g converges, then integral f converges; if integral f diverges to infinity, then integral g diverges to infinity.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the Comparison Test to prove an improper integral converges, without evaluating it exactly.
question_archetypes.answer: Split at x=1: on [0,1], e^(-x^2)<=1 so the piece is finite; on [1,infinity), e^(-x^2)<=e^(-x) and integral_1^infinity e^(-x)dx=1/e converges. Both pieces converge, so the whole converges.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integral cannot be evaluated exactly (no elementary antiderivative) but convergence can be established by bounding above by a known convergent integral, chosen to be larger everywhere on the relevant piece.
method_plan: Split the integral if needed so each piece has one clear source of (potential) impropriety
Find a known convergent comparison function that is >= the integrand on that piece
Conclude convergence via the Comparison Test
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct choice of comparison function that bounds the integrand ABOVE
M1: correct verification the comparison function's integral converges
A1: correct conclusion invoking the Comparison Test explicitly

common_errors.description: Choosing a comparison function that is smaller (not larger) than the integrand when trying to prove convergence — the inequality must point the right way
Not explicitly citing the Comparison Test as justification

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the Comparison Test to prove an improper integral diverges, by bounding it BELOW by a known divergent integral.
question_archetypes.answer: For x>=1, sqrt(x+1)<=sqrt(2x), so 1/sqrt(x+1) >= 1/sqrt(2x) = (1/sqrt2)*x^(-1/2); integral_1^infinity x^(-1/2)dx diverges (p=1/2<1), so by comparison the given integral diverges too.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: To prove divergence via comparison, the integrand must be shown to be LARGER than (or equal to) a known divergent function, the opposite inequality direction from the convergence case.
method_plan: Find a known divergent comparison function that is <= the integrand throughout the relevant interval
Verify the inequality carefully
Conclude divergence via the Comparison Test
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct choice of comparison function that bounds the integrand BELOW
M1: correct verification the comparison function's integral diverges
A1: correct conclusion invoking the Comparison Test explicitly

common_errors.description: Misapplying the comparison test with the inequality pointing the wrong way for a divergence proof

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine convergence of an improper integral by finding the dominant asymptotic power (big-O comparison) as x->infinity or near a finite singularity, without an explicit inequality.
question_archetypes.answer: As x->infinity, (x^2+1)/(x^4+x+1) ~ x^2/x^4 = x^(-2), so f(x)=O(x^-2) with p=2>1: converges by comparison to a p-integral.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: For a rational or algebraic integrand, identifying the leading-order behavior (highest powers) as x->infinity (or as x-> the singular point) quickly determines the effective p to compare against, without constructing an explicit inequality.
method_plan: Identify the dominant terms in numerator and denominator as x approaches the point of interest
Determine the effective power p of the asymptotic x^(-p) behavior
Apply the p-integral threshold to conclude convergence or divergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of dominant asymptotic terms
M1: correct effective power p determined
A1: correct convergence/divergence conclusion, ideally with a brief justification of the underlying inequality

common_errors.description: Using the leading term of the numerator or denominator alone without confirming the full asymptotic ratio
Stating the asymptotic power without ever tying it back to a rigorous comparison inequality when one is required

micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute the Trapezoid Rule approximation T_n for a definite integral, from a formula or from tabulated data
definitions: Partition [a,b] into n equal subintervals, h=(b-a)/n, x_j=a+jh, y_j=f(x_j). The Trapezoid Rule: T_n = h*( (1/2)y_0 + y_1 + y_2 + ... + y_(n-1) + (1/2)y_n ).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute T_n for a given function and n, comparing to the exact value if known.
question_archetypes.example: Compute T_4 for integral_1^2 dx/x (exact value ln2 approx 0.693147).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem specifies a function, interval, and n for the Trapezoid Rule specifically — apply the endpoint-half-weighted sum formula directly.
method_plan: Compute h=(b-a)/n and the partition points x_0,...,x_n
Evaluate y_j=f(x_j) at each partition point
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct h and partition points
M1: correct function values computed
A1: correct application of the weighted sum formula, correct final value

common_errors.description: Using the plain (unweighted) sum of all y-values instead of halving y_0 and y_n
Arithmetic slip evaluating one of the function values

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute T_n given only a table of (x,y) data values (no explicit formula for f).
question_archetypes.example: Given equally-spaced data y_0=2.1, y_1=2.4, y_2=2.9, y_3=3.5, y_4=4.0 with h=0.5, compute T_4.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Only tabulated y-values (no formula) are given — the Trapezoid Rule applies identically, just using the given data directly.
method_plan: Confirm the data points are equally spaced with the given h
Apply T_n=h*((1/2)y_0+y_1+...+y_(n-1)+(1/2)y_n) directly to the tabulated values
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of h and the endpoint-weighting pattern
A1: correct final computed value

common_errors.description: Assuming a formula for f is needed and failing to apply the rule directly from data

micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute the Midpoint Rule approximation M_n, and combine T_n, M_n to get T_2n without new function evaluations
definitions: With midpoints m_j=a+(j-1/2)h: M_n = h*(f(m_1)+f(m_2)+...+f(m_n)).
Relationship: T_2n = (T_n+M_n)/2 — lets already-computed T_n, M_n values be reused instead of recomputing T_2n from scratch.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute M_n for a given function and n.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem specifies the Midpoint Rule directly — evaluate f at the midpoints of each subinterval, not the endpoints.
method_plan: Compute h=(b-a)/n and the midpoints m_j=a+(j-1/2)h
Evaluate f at each midpoint
Sum and multiply by h

M1: correct function values at the midpoints
A1: correct final sum multiplied by h

common_errors.description: Evaluating f at the endpoints x_j instead of the true midpoints m_j
Arithmetic slip computing one of the midpoint values a+(j-1/2)h

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given T_n and M_n already computed, find T_2n using the relationship T_2n=(T_n+M_n)/2, without recomputing 2n new endpoint values.
question_archetypes.example: Given T_4 approx 0.697024 and M_4 approx 0.691220, find T_8.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: T_n and M_n at the same n are both already known — this exact relationship reconstructs T_2n for free, avoiding recomputing an entirely new set of function values.
method_plan: Confirm T_n and M_n are computed at the same n
Apply T_2n=(T_n+M_n)/2 directly
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification and application of the T_2n=(T_n+M_n)/2 relationship
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Recomputing T_2n from scratch with 2n+1 new function evaluations instead of using the free relationship
Trying to reuse Midpoint Rule data across different n directly (M_n data cannot be recycled into M_2n the way T_n can be combined into T_2n) — confusing this with the M_2n case

micro_skills.subtopic: Error Bounds for Trapezoid and Midpoint Rules
micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute and interpret the error bounds for T_n and M_n using a bound K on |f''|, and reason about concavity-based bracketing
definitions: If f'' is continuous on [a,b] and |f''(x)|<=K there: |integral_a^b f dx - T_n| <= K(b-a)^3/(12n^2), and |integral_a^b f dx - M_n| <= K(b-a)^3/(24n^2) — the Midpoint bound is about half the Trapezoid bound, and both are O(1/n^2).

theorems.name: Trapezoid/Midpoint Error Bound
conditions: K is any valid upper bound for |f''| on [a,b]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given f, [a,b], and n, find K=max|f''| and compute the error bound for T_n (or M_n).
question_archetypes.example: For integral_1^2 dx/x with n=4: f''(x)=2/x^3, K=max_{[1,2]}|f''|=2. Find the T_4 error bound.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for a BOUND on the error (not the actual error) — requires finding K=max|f''| on the interval, then substituting into the error-bound formula.
method_plan: Differentiate f twice to find f''
Find K=max|f''(x)| on [a,b] (often at an endpoint for monotonic f'')
Substitute K, (b-a), and n into the appropriate error-bound formula
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f'' computed
M1: correct K found as the max of |f''| on the interval
A1: correct substitution into the error-bound formula and final numeric bound

common_errors.description: Treating the computed error bound as if it were the actual (exact) error
Using the wrong power of n or (b-a) in the formula

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a target accuracy, solve the error-bound inequality for the minimum n needed.
question_archetypes.example: Find the minimum n so that T_n approximates integral_1^2 dx/x to within 10^-6, given K=2.
question_archetypes.answer: Solve 2*1/(12n^2) <= 10^-6 for n: n^2 >= 1/(6*10^-6), n >= about 408.25, so n=409 (or the next even/appropriate integer as required).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A target error tolerance is given and n is the unknown — set the error-bound formula less than or equal to the tolerance and solve the resulting inequality for n.
method_plan: Set up the error-bound inequality K(b-a)^3/(12n^2) <= tolerance (or the Midpoint analogue)
Solve algebraically for n
Round UP to the next integer (and to the required parity if applicable) since n must be a whole number satisfying the bound
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct inequality set up with the given tolerance
M1: correct algebraic solving for n
A1: correct rounding up to a valid integer n

common_errors.description: Rounding n down instead of up, giving an n that does not actually satisfy the required tolerance

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the concavity of f to reason about whether T_n over- or under-estimates the true integral (and vice versa for M_n), without computing an exact bound.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why, for f(x)=1/x on [1,2] (concave up), T_4 over-estimates and M_4 under-estimates integral_1^2 f dx.
question_archetypes.answer: For a concave-up function, chords lie above the curve, so the trapezoid areas over-estimate; the midpoint tangent-line rectangles lie below a concave-up curve, so they under-estimate. Thus T_n and M_n bracket the true value from opposite sides.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A qualitative question about which rule over/under-estimates (rather than a numeric bound) signals reasoning from the sign of f'' (concavity) directly.
method_plan: Determine the sign of f'' (concave up or down) on the interval
Reason geometrically: concave up means chords (trapezoids) lie above the curve and midpoint tangent rectangles lie below, or vice versa for concave down
State which rule over-estimates and which under-estimates
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct determination of concavity
A1: correct geometric reasoning identifying which rule over/under-estimates

common_errors.description: Getting the direction backwards (claiming concave-up makes the Trapezoid Rule under-estimate)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute Simpson's Rule approximation S_n (n even), applying the 1-4-2-4-...-4-1 weight pattern
definitions: Simpson's Rule approximates f on each pair of subintervals by a parabola through three consecutive points, and requires n EVEN: S_n = (h/3)*(y_0+4y_1+2y_2+4y_3+2y_4+...+2y_(n-2)+4y_(n-1)+y_n).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute S_n for a given function and even n.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: n is specified as even and Simpson's Rule is requested — apply the 1,4,2,4,...,4,1 weighting pattern rather than the Trapezoid or Midpoint weights.
method_plan: Compute h=(b-a)/n and all y_j=f(x_j)
Apply the weight pattern: endpoints get weight 1, odd-indexed interior points get weight 4, even-indexed interior points get weight 2
Multiply the weighted sum by h/3
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct h and all y_j computed
M1: correct 1-4-2-4-...-4-1 weight pattern applied
A1: correct final value, h/3 factor included

common_errors.description: Mis-assigning the weight pattern (e.g. giving an even-indexed interior point weight 4 instead of 2)
Using an odd n, for which Simpson's Rule as stated does not apply

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute S_n from a table of equally-spaced data values (no explicit formula for f), including a stated error bound from a given K.
question_archetypes.answer: S_4 = 2.2132, with error bound < 0.0049, so the true value lies in (2.2083, 2.2181).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Tabulated data with 5 equally-spaced values (n=4, even) signals direct application of Simpson's weight pattern to the raw data, plus a separately-stated error bound from the given K.
method_plan: Apply the 1-4-2-4-1 weight pattern directly to the 5 tabulated values
Multiply by h/3 for S_4
Substitute the given K into the Simpson error-bound formula to bracket the true value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct weighted sum from the table
M1: correct S_4 value with h/3 factor
A1: correct error bound computed and used to bracket the true value

common_errors.description: Misapplying the weight pattern to an odd number of data points, or to data that isn't actually equally spaced

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that Simpson's Rule requires n even, and adjust (or explain why a given n cannot be used directly) when n is odd.
question_archetypes.example: A student is asked to compute S_5 for integral_0^1 f(x)dx. Explain the issue.
question_archetypes.answer: Simpson's Rule (in the standard pairing form) requires n even, since each parabola spans 2 subintervals; n=5 does not divide evenly into pairs, so S_5 as stated is not directly defined — n must be increased to an even number (e.g. 6) or a composite rule used.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Before applying Simpson's Rule, always confirm n is even — an odd n is a red flag that the problem needs restating or a different n chosen.
method_plan: Check whether n is even
If odd, note the issue explicitly and use the nearest valid even n (or explain why the rule cannot be applied as stated)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification that n must be even for Simpson's Rule
A1: correct resolution (choosing a valid even n or clearly explaining the constraint)

common_errors.description: Attempting to apply the standard Simpson weight pattern with an odd n regardless

micro_skills.subtopic: Simpson's Rule Error Bound and Relationships to T_n, M_n
micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute the Simpson error bound via f'''', relate S_2n to T_n and M_n, and reason about exactness for low-degree polynomials
definitions: If f'''' is continuous on [a,b] and |f''''(x)|<=K: |integral_a^b f dx - S_n| <= K(b-a)^5/(180n^4) — error is O(1/n^4), much faster than Trapezoid/Midpoint's O(1/n^2). Simpson's Rule is EXACT for any polynomial of degree <=3, since f''''=0 identically for such polynomials.
Relationship to T_n, M_n: S_2n = (T_n+2M_n)/3 = (2T_2n+M_n)/3 = (4T_2n-T_n)/3.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given f, [a,b], and n, find K=max|f''''| and compute the Simpson error bound.
question_archetypes.example: For integral_1^2 dx/x with n=4: f''''(x)=24/x^5, K=24. Find the S_4 error bound.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for a Simpson error BOUND — requires finding K=max|f''''| on the interval and substituting into the (b-a)^5/(180n^4) formula.
method_plan: Differentiate f four times to find f''''
Find K=max|f''''(x)| on [a,b]
Substitute into the Simpson error-bound formula
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f'''' computed
M1: correct K found
A1: correct substitution and final numeric bound

common_errors.description: Error computing the fourth derivative, especially sign/coefficient tracking across four differentiations
Using n^2 instead of n^4 in the denominator (confusing with the Trapezoid/Midpoint bound)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain (conceptually) why Simpson's Rule is exact for cubic polynomials but not necessarily for quartics, tying the reasoning to the error-bound formula.
question_archetypes.example: If a numerical scheme is exact for all cubics, is it necessarily exact for all quartics? Relate to Simpson's Rule.
question_archetypes.answer: Not necessarily. Simpson's error bound involves f''''; for a cubic, f''''=0 identically, forcing zero error. For a quartic, f'''' is a nonzero constant, so the error bound does not force exactness — Simpson's Rule is generally NOT exact for quartics, only guaranteed to have error that vanishes at rate O(h^4).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A conceptual question about exactness for a given polynomial degree should be answered by checking whether the relevant derivative in the error-bound formula (here f'''') is identically zero for that degree.
method_plan: Identify which derivative order appears in the error-bound formula (f'''' for Simpson)
Check whether that derivative is identically zero for the polynomial degree in question
Conclude exactness only when that derivative vanishes identically, not merely because the error bound is small
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification that f''''=0 for cubics but not quartics
A1: correct conceptual conclusion (exact for cubics, not necessarily exact for quartics) with justification

common_errors.description: Assuming exactness for a lower degree automatically implies exactness for a higher degree

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given T_n and M_n already computed, find S_2n using the relationship S_2n=(T_n+2M_n)/3, without recomputing from scratch.
question_archetypes.example: Given T_4 approx 0.7828 and M_4 approx 0.7867 for integral_0^1 dx/(1+x^2), find S_8 (equivalently labeled S_4 in the n-pairs-of-subintervals convention used).
question_archetypes.answer: S = (T_4+2*M_4)/3 = (0.7828+2(0.7867))/3 approx 0.7854, matching pi/4 to 4 decimal places
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: T_n and M_n at the same n are both already known — this relationship reconstructs the Simpson approximation for free.
method_plan: Confirm T_n and M_n are computed at the same n
Apply S=(T_n+2M_n)/3 directly
Compare to the exact value if known, to illustrate the improved accuracy
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification and application of the S=(T_n+2M_n)/3 relationship
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Misremembering the relationship as (2T_n+M_n)/3 instead of (T_n+2M_n)/3

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply a smoothing substitution before numerical integration when the integrand or its derivatives are unbounded near an endpoint, and map infinite intervals to finite ones
definitions: If f or its derivatives are unbounded near an endpoint (even if the integral itself is proper, or improper-but-convergent), a substitution can smooth the integrand so the stated O(1/n^2) or O(1/n^4) error bounds actually hold.
For an infinite interval, a substitution (e.g. x=1/t) maps it to a finite interval before applying Trapezoid/Simpson.
formulas: x=t^2 (or similar) can smooth an integrand with unbounded derivatives near an endpoint; x=1/t maps an infinite interval to a finite one

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an integral whose integrand has unbounded derivatives near an endpoint, apply a substitution to smooth it before recommending a numerical method.
question_archetypes.example: For integral_0^1 sqrt(x)*e^x dx, substitute x=t^2 to smooth the integrand before applying Simpson's Rule.
question_archetypes.answer: Substituting x=t^2, dx=2t dt gives 2*integral_0^1 t^2*e^(t^2) dt, whose integrand has bounded derivatives near t=0, unlike sqrt(x)*e^x near x=0.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An integrand with a fractional power (like sqrt(x)) at an endpoint has unbounded higher derivatives there, which would silently invalidate the usual O(1/n^2)/O(1/n^4) numerical error bounds unless smoothed first.
method_plan: Identify the endpoint where the integrand's derivatives are unbounded
Choose a substitution (e.g. x=t^2) that removes the problematic fractional power
Rewrite the integral in the new variable, confirming the new integrand has bounded derivatives near the relevant point
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the problematic endpoint behavior
M1: correct substitution chosen and applied
A1: correct confirmation the new integrand is smooth enough for the numerical method's error bound to hold

common_errors.description: Applying a numerical method directly to the unsmoothed integrand, causing the stated convergence rate to fail silently (converging much more slowly than the formula predicts)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Map an improper integral over an infinite interval to a finite interval via a substitution, in preparation for applying Trapezoid/Simpson numerically.
question_archetypes.example: Map integral_1^infinity e^(-x)/x^2 dx to a finite interval using x=1/t.
question_archetypes.answer: With x=1/t, dx=-dt/t^2, the limits x=1 to infinity become t=1 to 0; the integral becomes integral_0^1 e^(-1/t) dt (after simplifying the t^2 factors), now over a finite interval suitable for Trapezoid/Simpson.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An infinite interval cannot be directly discretized into finitely many subintervals for Trapezoid/Simpson — a substitution like x=1/t remaps it to a finite interval first.
method_plan: Choose a substitution (commonly x=1/t) that sends the infinite endpoint to a finite value
Rewrite dx and the limits in terms of the new variable
Simplify the resulting integral over the new finite interval, checking for any new endpoint singularities introduced
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution and transformed limits
M1: correct rewritten integrand and differential
A1: correct final finite-interval integral, with any new singularity noted

common_errors.description: Forgetting to transform dx as well as the limits, leaving an inconsistent integral
Not checking whether the substitution introduces a NEW singularity (e.g. at t=0) that also needs smoothing

micro_skills.micro_skill: Build a Romberg table from Trapezoid estimates at doubled subdivision counts, using Richardson extrapolation to accelerate convergence
definitions: Since I-T_n = C_1/n^2 + C_2/n^4 + ... , combining Trapezoid estimates at doubled n cancels the leading error term: T^1_(k+1) = (4*T^0_(k+1) - T^0_k)/3 (equal to S_(2^(k+1))), and generally T^j_k = (4^j*T^(j-1)_k - T^(j-1)_(k-1))/(4^j-1). The diagonal entries R_j=T^j_j converge extremely fast, each column eliminating one more power of 1/n^2 in the error.

theorems.name: Romberg recursion (Richardson extrapolation)
theorems.statement: T^j_k = (4^j*T^(j-1)_k - T^(j-1)_(k-1)) / (4^j - 1), building each new column from the column directly to its left.
conditions: the base column T^0_k = T_(2^k) consists of Trapezoid estimates at doubled subdivision counts

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a sequence of Trapezoid estimates T_1, T_2, T_4, T_8, ..., build the first one or two extra columns of the Romberg table.
question_archetypes.example: Given T_1=0.75, T_2 approx 0.708333, T_4 approx 0.697024, T_8 approx 0.694122 for integral_1^2 dx/x, compute R_1=(4T_2-T_1)/3 and R_2 using the next column.
question_archetypes.answer: R_1(from T_1,T_2) approx 0.694444 (=S_2); further entries R_2 approx 0.693175, converging toward ln2 approx 0.693147
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A sequence of Trapezoid estimates at successively doubled n is given — apply the Romberg recursion column by column to accelerate convergence toward the true value.
method_plan: Arrange the given T_(2^k) values as the base column of the table
Apply T^1_k=(4T^0_k-T^0_(k-1))/3 to build the first extrapolated column
Continue to further columns with the general formula T^j_k=(4^j T^(j-1)_k - T^(j-1)_(k-1))/(4^j-1) if requested
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct base column identified
M1: correct application of the column-1 Romberg formula
A1: correct numeric values in the extrapolated column(s)

common_errors.description: Mixing up rows and columns — each new entry uses the one directly above and the one to its upper-left, not values from other rows entirely
Using the wrong power of 4 (4^j) for the column being computed

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply the general Romberg recursion T^j_k=(4^j T^(j-1)_k - T^(j-1)_(k-1))/(4^j-1) to compute a specific higher-order table entry.
question_archetypes.example: Given the first-column Romberg entries R^1_2 approx 0.694444 and R^1_3 approx 0.693175, compute the second-column entry R^2_3 = (16*R^1_3 - R^1_2)/15.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives entries from an earlier column and asks for the next column — apply the general formula with j incremented, using 4^j (not always 4) as the weighting power.
method_plan: Identify j (the column being computed) and the two required entries from the previous column
Apply T^j_k=(4^j T^(j-1)_k - T^(j-1)_(k-1))/(4^j-1) with the correct power of 4
State the resulting more accurate estimate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of j and the two required prior entries
M1: correct application of the formula with the correct 4^j weight
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Using 4^1 instead of the correct 4^j for a column beyond the first

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain the relationship between the first Romberg column and Simpson's Rule, and reason about when higher-order methods might not outperform Trapezoid.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why the first Romberg column entry from T_n and T_2n equals S_2n, and give a case where Simpson/Romberg's higher-order error bound might not apply.
question_archetypes.answer: The formula (4T_2n-T_n)/3 is algebraically identical to S_2n, so the first Romberg column reproduces Simpson's Rule exactly. Higher-order bounds (O(1/n^4) for Simpson, faster still for Romberg) require enough continuous derivatives (f'''' continuous, bounded); if f has unbounded higher derivatives or sign changes making |f''''| large/undefined, the stated fast-convergence bounds may not hold, and cruder methods might do comparably.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A conceptual question linking the Romberg table's first column to Simpson's Rule, or asking when higher-order numerical methods fail to outperform Trapezoid, should be answered by referencing the derivative-smoothness conditions each error bound requires.
method_plan: Show algebraically that (4T_2n-T_n)/3 = S_2n
Recall that each method's fast-convergence guarantee (O(1/n^2), O(1/n^4), etc.) depends on the relevant derivative being continuous and bounded
Identify when that smoothness assumption might fail, undermining the expected speed advantage
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct algebraic demonstration that the first Romberg column equals Simpson's Rule
A1: correct identification of the smoothness assumption underlying the higher-order bounds and when it can fail

common_errors.description: Assuming Romberg/Simpson always beats Trapezoid regardless of the smoothness of f, without checking the derivative-boundedness hypotheses
